Banchan / Heritage

Yeongeun Jorim Soy-Braised Lotus Root

Lotus root, cut into coins, braised in soy and sweetness until the holes fill with glaze and the flesh turns amber-tender: yeongeun jorim is the banchan that looks like architecture and eats like comfort.

Korean · Medium · Serves 4–6 as banchan

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 03 / 25 banchan recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the elegant braise. Lotus root, cut into coins, braised in soy and sweetness until the holes fill with glaze and the flesh turns amber-tender: yeongeun jorim is the banchan that looks like architecture and eats like comfort. The coin's lace of holes catches the braise in every bite — the visual is the recipe's promise — and the long braise turns a crunchy raw root into something tender-firm and deeply savory. It is the jorim family's most elegant member, and the patient one: the braise runs half an hour and cannot be rushed.

The lotus root
The braise

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Peel, cut, and soak at once — lotus root oxidizes to gray-brown in minutes, and the vinegar-water soak (10 minutes while the rest comes together) keeps the coins snowy and leaches a little starch so the braise glazes instead of gumming.
  • Check each coin's holes: a quick rinse pokes out the mud that lives in the channels of field-fresh roots.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    The coins and everything but the sesame finish into a wide pan — soy, water, syrup, mirin, garlic, chili — brought to a simmer, lid on, medium-low. Checkpoint — a gentle bubble, not a boil: the braise should barely tremble. A hard boil breaks the coins' shape before they tender.
  2. 02
    Braise 25–30 minutes, turning the coins once at the halfway mark, lid on until the last five minutes. The braise reduces slowly while the root drinks. Checkpoint — the doneness read: a paring knife or chopstick slides into a coin's flesh with gentle resistance — tender-firm, never soft, and the thinnest coins' edges have gone translucent amber. The braise by now has reduced to a syrup that pools in the pan's low spots.
  3. 03
    Lid off, the final reduction — 5 minutes, turning the coins through the thickening syrup every 60 seconds until every face wears glaze and the pan is nearly dry. Off the heat: sesame oil, seeds. Checkpoint — the coin test: bite through and the holes should visibly hold glaze; the flesh gives with a fine, almost crisp-firm grain (lotus keeps a faint snap even fully braised — its signature), savory-sweet through and through. Chef’s Note — lotus root's texture law is the reverse of the potato's (#B09): potato goes fully soft in the braise and would vanish at thirty minutes, while lotus holds its firm-crisp grain at an hour — the two jorim roots sit on opposite ends of the starch-spectrum, which is why a holiday banchan table carries both. The lotus coin's beauty survives the braise precisely because of that structure; it is the banchan you plate first and everyone photographs before eating.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Coins gray-brownNo vinegar soakPeel-cut-soak as one motion
Coins broke apartHard boil or over-braisedThe trembling simmer; tender-firm pull
Glaze gummed, cloudyStarch not leachedThe full 10-minute soak before the pan
Bland in the centerShort braise or thick coinsEven 1 cm; the full 25–30

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 4–5 days refrigerated and improves for two days as the coins keep drinking — the elegant make-ahead. Serve at room temperature or lightly warmed; the glaze is best not reheated hard.
  • Variations: the same braise on potato (#B09) and quail eggs (#B19); honey swapped in runs a deeper gold; a garnish of julienned red chili over the coins for the holiday table's full architecture.
